question: Which of the following can be blocked by atropine, a muscarinic receptor blocker?

options.opa: Increased blood pressure caused by nicotine
options.opb: Increased skeletal muscle strength caused by neostigmine, an acetycholine esterase inhibitor
options.opc: Bradycardia caused by infusion of acetylcholine

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Atropine" -> "blocks muscarinic receptors" -> "prevents acetylcholine action on heart" -> "prevents bradycardia" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Atropine" -> "blocks muscarinic receptors" -> "no effect on nicotinic receptors" -> "no effect on nicotine-induced blood pressure increase" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Atropine" -> "blocks muscarinic receptors" -> "no effect on skeletal muscle" -> "no effect on neostigmine-induced muscle strength increase" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Atropine" -> "blocks muscarinic receptors" -> "prevents acetylcholine action on heart" -> "prevents bradycardia" -> "no effect on nicotine or neostigmine actions" -> 85%
analysis: Atropine is a muscarinic receptor blocker, which means it specifically inhibits the action of acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors. Muscarinic receptors are involved in various parasympathetic nervous system responses, including heart rate regulation. Bradycardia, or a slowed heart rate, caused by acetylcholine infusion is mediated through muscarinic receptors. Therefore, atropine can effectively block this effect. On the other hand, increased blood pressure caused by nicotine and increased skeletal muscle strength caused by neostigmine are mediated through nicotinic receptors, which atropine does not affect. Nicotine acts on nicotinic receptors in the autonomic ganglia and adrenal medulla, while neostigmine enhances skeletal muscle contraction by inhibiting acetylcholine breakdown at the neuromuscular junction, which also involves nicotinic receptors. Thus, atropine cannot block these effects. Based on this understanding, the most likely correct option is that atropine can block bradycardia caused by acetylcholine infusion.
